opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic puzzle is this. When you look inside a model and try to find a neuron that means one thing, you mostly don't. You find neurons that fire for a weird mix of unrelated concepts: some academic citations, some Korean text, some HTTP requests. They're polysemantic. Superposition is the best explanation we have for why that happens.

The intuition goes like this. The model wants to represent far more concepts, or features, than it has dimensions. Think of everything a language model might need to track: every person, place, programming construct, grammatical role, tone. That's easily millions of things, and it only has a few thousand dimensions in the residual stream at any layer. If it gave each feature its own neuron, it would run out of room almost immediately.

What it does instead is pack features in as directions that are *almost* orthogonal rather than perfectly orthogonal. In high-dimensional spaces you can fit exponentially more nearly-orthogonal directions than you have dimensions. The cost is a bit of interference: when one feature is active, it leaks a little onto others that share some overlap.

The key thing that makes this work is sparsity. Most features are off most of the time. On any given token, the model isn't simultaneously thinking about the French Revolution, Python decorators, and sourdough recipes. Because only a handful of features are active at once, the interference stays small, and the model can use nonlinearities to clean up the noise. So it's a trade: you accept a little crosstalk in exchange for vastly more capacity. Toy-model work showed this pretty cleanly. As you make features sparser, models flip from representing a few features cleanly to cramming in many more features in superposition.

For interpretability, this is both bad news and good news. The bad news is that neurons aren't the right unit of analysis. If you stare at individual neurons, you're looking at a projection of many features at once, so you'll get confusing results. The good news is that if superposition is the right story, there *is* a cleaner basis hidden in there. The features are real directions; they just aren't aligned with the neurons.

That's what motivates tools like sparse autoencoders, or transcoders and cross-layer transcoders, which we've leaned on a lot for circuit tracing. You train a wider dictionary with a sparsity penalty to try to recover those underlying directions. When it works, you get features that are much more interpretable, like a feature for "Golden Gate Bridge" or for "the token is inside a rhyme scheme," and you can start tracing how they interact to produce a behavior.

I'd add a caveat. Superposition is a really useful frame, but I don't think it's the whole story. The features we pull out depend on dictionary size and training choices. Features split into finer ones as you scale up the dictionary, and there's a nontrivial chunk of the model's computation we still can't explain, sometimes called the "dark matter." So I'd think of it as our best working hypothesis for why representations are dense and messy. It's been productive in practice, but it's still being refined as we look closer.

r001.rationale: It says the model represents “far more concepts, or features, than it has dimensions” and explains that this leads to packing features into the representation.

r002.rationale: It describes features as directions in a high-dimensional space and says they are not aligned with individual neurons, communicating that a feature spans the representation rather than mapping to one neuron.

r003.rationale: It says sparse autoencoders and related tools are used to recover the underlying feature directions, yielding more interpretable features. This communicates the goal of recovering monosemantic representations from superposed ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about superposition is really as the answer to a puzzle you run into very quickly when you start looking inside these models. If you take a neuron in a language model and you ask, "what does this neuron do?", a lot of the time the honest answer is "a bunch of things." It fires on, say, Korean text, and also on the end of a URL, and also on some specific grammatical construction. And that's frustrating if you were hoping neurons were the natural units of computation, because they just don't line up with concepts the way you'd want.

So the superposition hypothesis is basically: the model wants to represent way more features than it has dimensions. The residual stream of a model might be a few thousand dimensions wide, but the number of things the model would like to keep track of—entities, syntax, tone, facts, all the little intermediate variables of its computation—is enormously larger than that. And the trick it uses is that it represents those features as directions that aren't orthogonal to each other. If you have N dimensions, you can only fit N perfectly orthogonal directions, but you can fit vastly more "almost orthogonal" directions. There's a nice geometry result there about how many nearly-orthogonal vectors you can pack into a high-dimensional space, and it's exponential in the dimension.

The cost of that is interference. If two features share some overlap in their directions, then when one is active, it looks a little bit like the other one is active too. And the reason the model can get away with that is sparsity. Most features aren't active most of the time. On any given token, only a tiny fraction of all the things the model could be thinking about are relevant, so the chance that two overlapping features are both on at once is low, and the interference is mostly noise the model can tolerate.

So when you see a dense, polysemantic neuron, superposition says: that neuron isn't the real unit. It's a basis direction that happens to have a bunch of features projected onto it at once. The features are still there, they're just not aligned with the neuron axes. And that reframing is really what motivated the whole dictionary learning and sparse autoencoder line of work, because if you believe the model is storing a big sparse dictionary of features in a compressed, overlapping way, then the natural thing to do is try to learn that dictionary and decompress it. You train something that takes the dense activations and finds a much larger set of sparsely-active directions that reconstruct them. And when you do that, you get a lot of things that are much more interpretable than the raw neurons—a feature for the Golden Gate Bridge, a feature for code that has a bug in it, that kind of thing.

I'd add one caveat, which is that superposition is a hypothesis about the model, not a proven fact, and it's probably an idealization. The toy models where we understand it cleanly have very clean sparsity and very clean feature structure, and real models are messier. There's also a lot we don't understand about how the model actually computes with features in superposition—it's one thing to store them that way, it's another to do a whole chain of reasoning while everything is overlapping. But as a lens, it's been enormously useful. It takes the thing that initially looks like a mess—dense, uninterpretable activations—and gives you a story for why that mess is actually expected, and a concrete path for unpacking it.

r001.rationale: It says the model represents “way more features than it has dimensions.”

r002.rationale: It describes features as directions in the representation that are not aligned with neuron axes, with their projections overlapping across neurons—communicating that features are distributed across dimensions.

r003.rationale: It describes dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders as learning a larger set of sparse directions to decompress dense activations and recover more interpretable features.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about superposition is that a model may want to represent more features than it has dimensions available. And it can do that because those features don’t all need to be active at the same time.

Imagine that you wanted to represent each concept with its own neuron. That’s a very clean scheme, but it’s expensive: every new feature needs another neuron. Instead, you can represent a feature as a direction across many neurons. Those directions don’t have to be perfectly orthogonal. They can overlap, as long as the interference is small enough that the model can still use them.

The key intuition is sparsity. For any particular input, only a small fraction of all the features the model knows about are relevant. That gives the model room to pack many more features into its representation than you might expect from the number of dimensions.

And that makes interpreting individual neurons difficult. A neuron might respond to several seemingly unrelated things because it participates in several different feature directions. So superposition gives us an explanation for why looking at neurons one at a time might not reveal the meaningful units of computation. We may need to find those directions instead.

r001.rationale: It says the model may represent more features than it has dimensions available.

r002.rationale: It explains that a feature can be represented as a direction across many neurons.

r003.rationale: It suggests finding feature directions, but does not identify recovering monosemantic representations as the goal of untangling superposition.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that a model may want to represent many more features than it has dimensions available. So instead of assigning each feature its own neuron, it represents features as directions in activation space, and those directions can overlap. That’s what we mean by superposition.

One intuition is that, in a high-dimensional space, you can fit a lot of directions that are almost orthogonal, even though they can’t all be perfectly orthogonal. If the features are sparse—if only a small fraction are active for any particular input—the model can tolerate the interference and still recover useful information.

That helps explain why looking at individual neurons can be confusing. A neuron might respond to several seemingly unrelated concepts because it participates in several overlapping representations. The meaningful unit may be a pattern across neurons rather than a single neuron.

I’d distinguish that hypothesis from the observation that representations are dense, though. Dense activations alone don’t establish superposition. The stronger claim is that the model is using overlapping directions to represent more features than it has dimensions, and understanding those features requires us to disentangle them.

r001.rationale: It says the model may represent more features than it has dimensions available.

r002.rationale: It describes features as directions in activation space that overlap, communicating that a feature is represented across the space rather than by one neuron.

r003.rationale: It says understanding features requires disentangling them, but does not identify recovering monosemantic representations as the goal.
